title: Prescription Assistance
subtitle: Follow the drug from prescription to formulary to final pharmacy cost

blocks.text: A prescription can fit on one screen. Getting it covered may take a formulary, a deductible, special approval and three people saying, “Let me check that.”

Public drug coverage comes mostly from provincial, territorial and federal programs, with private plans on top. National pharmacare deals now cover listed birth control and diabetes products in the provinces and territories that signed on. Other medicines still follow local drug plans, drug lists and approval rules.
National pharmacare is not yet one list for every medicine in every province. It covers listed products where there is a deal, and local public drug plans still matter a lot.

items.title: “A provincial health card automatically pays for every outpatient prescription.”
items.text: Coverage for hospital and doctor visits is not the same as coverage for every drug at the pharmacy. Whether you qualify, whether you signed up and the drug list still matter.

blocks.text: Health Canada: National pharmacare coverage
Knowing who pays for your medicine, and how, keeps a surprise bill from putting your treatment at risk.
blocks.detail: The right plan, the drug list and a few price layers decide what you pay at the counter.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you find who pays first.

sections.title: Ask Who Pays Before You Ask How Much

blocks.text: Find out who pays before you price the medicine. A claim sent to the wrong door rarely comes back on time.

items.title: PUBLIC PLAN
items.text: Check provincial or territorial plans for seniors, children, people on income support, high drug costs, specific illnesses or coverage based on income.

items.title: FEDERAL PROGRAM
items.text: First Nations and Inuit clients who qualify, veterans, military members, federal workers, refugees and others may have a federal plan with its own rules.

items.title: PRIVATE PLAN
items.text: Coverage through work, a union, retirement, school or your own policy may pay first or work alongside a public plan.

items.title: PATIENT HELP PROGRAMS
items.text: Drug makers or charities may help in some cases. Check the privacy terms, how long it lasts and what happens when the help ends.

blocks.text: Ontario’s Trillium Drug Program helps households whose drug costs are high compared to their income. Ontario Drug Benefit coverage still follows its drug list and Exceptional Access rules.
Alberta Non-Group Coverage is an optional extra plan for residents under 65 who qualify, and it has a monthly premium. Alberta seniors have a separate plan with no premium.

items.title: “If one province covers a drug, every province must cover it.”
items.text: Each province has its own drug list, medical criteria and approval system. Drug names cross borders more easily than payment rules.

blocks.text: Ontario: Prescription drug coverage

sections.title: Covered Can Still Have Four Price Layers

blocks.text: Read the receipt like a drug list, not a mood.

items.title: Formulary status
items.text: Is this exact drug, strength and form on your plan’s list, and is a lower-cost version covered instead?

items.title: Deductible
items.text: How much do you pay yourself each year before the plan starts sharing the cost?

items.title: Co-payment
items.text: After the deductible, what flat fee or percentage do you pay for each fill?

items.title: Maximum
items.text: Is there a yearly family maximum after which the plan pays more, or a limit on what the plan will pay?

blocks.text: B.C. Fair PharmaCare uses family income to set your deductible and family maximum. You have to register and agree to an income check to get coverage matched to your income.
Special Authority or Exceptional Access is usually sent in by the prescriber and checked against medical criteria. Even with approval, you may still owe a deductible or co-payment.

items.title: “Special authorization means the medicine will be free.”
items.text: It can make the drug eligible for the plan to pay. Deductibles, co-payments, price rules and other plans may still apply. Approval opens the door. It does not pay the parking.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: getting help with drug costs means matching the drug to the right plan. Check the exact drug, plan, drug list, approval, deductible and pharmacy cost before you assume it is covered or stop taking it.
B.C.: Fair PharmaCare plan

sections.title: Dev and the Approval That Still Had a Deductible

blocks.text: Meet Dev
paragraphs: Dev Sharma lives in Surrey and has just been approved for a new medicine for his heart. His goal is to start it this week, as his doctor asked. The approval letter says his plan will now cover it.
At the pharmacy, Dev expects to pay nothing. The receipt, having received no such instructions, shows $310.
Dev is stunned. That is most of his grocery money for the month. He thinks about leaving the bag on the counter and trying again next month.

Instead, he asks the pharmacist one question: why? The pharmacist explains. The approval made the drug eligible, but Dev has not paid his Fair PharmaCare deductible yet this year. His income on file is also two years old, from when he earned more.

Dev decides not to skip the medicine. He pays for a one-week supply he can afford and asks his doctor about a lower-cost option the plan also covers. Then he updates his income with Fair PharmaCare that night.
The twist comes a week later. With his lower income on file, his deductible drops sharply. His next refill costs far less, and he knows exactly when the plan will pay more.
The medicine does not become magically free. The cost becomes something he can trace, and Dev has a plan for the deductible, the renewal and the next refill instead of a surprise at the counter.

blocks.text: A sudden high price can come from an expired approval, a reset deductible, old income details, a different product or two plans not talking. Ask what changed before you give up on the prescription.
What resolved the conflict?
Approval and payment are separate steps. Check the deductible, your income details and the family maximum before you expect to pay nothing.
Dev kept taking his heart medicine by asking why it cost $310 instead of walking away from the counter.
blocks.detail: One question to your pharmacist can turn a shocking price into a plan you can afford.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is your health card not proof that pharmacy drugs are covered?
items.detail: Coverage for hospital and doctor visits is not the same as coverage for every drug at the pharmacy. Whether you qualify, signing up and the drug list still matter.

items.title: Which four kinds of payer should you check?
items.detail: A public plan, a federal program, a private plan and patient help programs.

items.title: What details must match the drug list?
items.detail: The exact drug, strength, form and approved use. A similar name is not always the same listing.

items.title: What does special approval do?
items.detail: It can make a limited drug eligible for the plan to pay. Deductibles, co-payments, price rules and other plans may still apply.

items.title: How is a deductible different from a co-payment?
items.detail: You pay the deductible yourself before the plan starts sharing costs. A co-payment is the flat fee or percentage you pay after coverage starts.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Prescription Coverage and Cost File

blocks.text: Use medicine and document names only. Do not write health card numbers, prescription numbers or health portal logins here.

Ask the pharmacist for the price before they fill it, and whether a lower-cost version is covered. Never skip, split, swap or stop a prescribed medicine only because of cost without first talking to a pharmacist or prescriber about safe options.

items.title: Formulary
items.text: The official list of drugs a plan covers, and its conditions.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: What you pay yourself before the plan starts sharing the cost.

items.title: Co-payment
items.text: Your flat fee or percentage for a covered claim.

items.title: Special authorization
items.text: Medical approval needed before a limited drug is covered.

items.title: Generic substitution
items.text: Using a lower-cost version that works the same, under plan rules.

items.title: Family maximum
items.text: The yearly amount after which the plan pays more of your costs.

items.title: Coordination of benefits
items.text: How two or more plans share one claim, and in what order.

quiz.question: True or False: “A provincial health card automatically pays for every outpatient prescription.”

questions: Which province or territory do you live in? Name your public drug plan if you know it.
Do you have other drug coverage, such as through work, school or a federal program? Write “none” if not.
Which medicine are you asking about? A name and strength are enough.
Did the pharmacy say it needs special approval or is not on the drug list? (Yes / No / Not sure)
About how much did you pay, or are you being asked to pay? An estimate is fine.
What is one question you will ask your pharmacist or plan?
samples: It needed Special Authority, and that was approved.
How much of my deductible is left this year?
